title: Number theory
summary: Primes, divisibility and modular arithmetic — the integer toolkit behind hashing, counting and cryptography.

articles.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
articles.summary: List every prime up to n by crossing out multiples instead of testing numbers one at a time.
articles.idea_md:
Testing numbers one at a time repeats work: trial division tries `2`, `3`, `5`, `7`, … against every candidate, over and over, even though each of those primes only ever rules out its own multiples. The sieve turns the question around. Instead of asking *"is this number prime?"* for every candidate, it asks *"which numbers does this prime rule out?"* and answers it once per prime.

Start with a table that marks every number from `2` to `n` as a candidate. Walk upward. The first unmarked number you meet is prime — nothing smaller divides it, or it would have been crossed out already. Cross out all of its multiples, then move on to the next unmarked number.

Two observations make it fast:

- **Start at `p * p`.** A multiple `k * p` with `k < p` has a smaller prime factor, so an earlier pass already removed it.
- **Stop at `√n`.** Once `p * p > n` there is nothing left to cross out; every number still unmarked is prime.

Each prime `p` touches about `n / p` cells, and summing that over the primes gives `O(n log log n)` — in practice a sieve up to ten million finishes in well under a second. Memory is one flag per number, which is why the table is usually a `vector<bool>` (bit-packed) or a byte array.
articles.applications_md:
- **Precomputing primes** for many queries: primality checks become a table lookup.
- **Counting and summing primes** in a range, or building prefix counts of primes.
- **Seeding other sieves**: the same crossing-out loop computes smallest prime factors, Euler's totient or the number of divisors for every number up to `n`.
- **Segmented sieving**: sieve `[L, R]` for huge `L` using only the primes up to `√R`.
articles.pitfall_md:
- Using `int` for `p * p` overflows once `n` approaches `2^31`; keep the loop variable 64-bit or compare `p <= n / p`.
- Allocate `n + 1` entries: the table is indexed by the numbers themselves, so `n` needs slot `n` — one short and the last write runs off the end.
- Crossing out from `2 * p` instead of `p * p` is still correct, just slower — but starting at `p` would mark `p` itself composite.
- A sieve up to `10^9` needs 125 MB even bit-packed, more than most judges allow; switch to a segmented sieve or a primality test.

articles.title: Smallest prime factor table
articles.summary: A sieve variant that factorizes any number up to n in O(log n) by following its smallest prime factor.
articles.idea_md:
The plain sieve answers *whether* a number is prime. Record a little more — for every number, the **smallest prime that divides it** — and the same pass lets you factorize any number in the table almost instantly.

Build the table like a sieve: walk `i` upward; if `spf[i]` is still empty, `i` is prime, so claim every multiple of `i` whose entry is still empty. Because primes are processed in increasing order, the first prime to claim a number is its smallest prime factor.

Factorizing `x` is then a short walk: `spf[x]` is one prime factor; divide it out and repeat on `x / spf[x]` until you reach `1`.

```
spf[360] = 2  →  180 → 90 → 45
spf[45]  = 3  →  15 → 5
spf[5]   = 5  →  1          360 = 2·2·2·3·3·5
```

Every step divides `x` by at least `2`, so a factorization takes at most `log₂ x` steps. The table costs one integer per number, which is the trade: `O(n)` memory for `O(log x)` factorizations instead of `O(√x)` trial division each time.
articles.formula: n = p_1^{e_1} \, p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_k^{e_k}, \qquad k \le \log_2 n
articles.applications_md:
- **Many factorizations**: counting divisors, summing divisors or computing Euler's totient for thousands of numbers.
- **Distinct prime factors** of every array element, e.g. to group numbers that share a factor.
- **Radicals and square-free checks**: a repeated factor shows up as the same `spf` twice in a row.
articles.pitfall_md:
- The table only covers numbers up to `n`; factorizing something larger needs trial division by the primes up to its square root.
- `spf` of `0` and `1` is undefined — guard the loop with `x > 1`.
- One `int` per number is 4 MB per million entries; for `10^8` that is 400 MB, too much for most judges.

articles.title: Binary exponentiation
articles.summary: Raise a number to the n-th power with O(log n) multiplications by squaring along the bits of n.
articles.idea_md:
Multiplying `a` by itself `n` times takes `n − 1` multiplications. Squaring is the shortcut: `a²` squared is `a⁴`, squared again is `a⁸`, so `k` squarings reach `a^(2^k)`. Any exponent is a sum of powers of two — its binary digits — so `a^n` is the product of the squares that correspond to the set bits of `n`.

`13 = 1101₂ = 8 + 4 + 1`, so `a^13 = a^8 · a^4 · a^1`.

Walk the bits of `n` from the lowest one up while keeping `base = a^(2^k)`:

1. If the current bit is set, multiply the result by `base`.
2. Square `base` and shift `n` right by one.

That is at most two multiplications per bit, `O(log n)` in total. Under a modulus, reduce after every multiplication so the numbers never outgrow the machine word.

The idea is not about numbers specifically — it works for anything with an associative multiplication. Raising the matrix `[[1, 1], [1, 0]]` to the `n`-th power yields Fibonacci numbers in `O(log n)`, and composing a permutation with itself `n` times works the same way.
articles.formula: a^{n} = \begin{cases} 1 & n = 0 \\ \left(a^{n/2}\right)^{2} & n \text{ even} \\ a \cdot a^{n-1} & n \text{ odd} \end{cases}
articles.applications_md:
- **Modular powers** in hashing, combinatorics (`n!` inverses via Fermat's little theorem) and primality tests.
- **Linear recurrences** such as Fibonacci or tiling counts: raise the recurrence's matrix to the `n`-th power.
- **Repeated application** of any associative step: composing a permutation, doubling in a graph ("where am I after `2^k` moves?").
articles.pitfall_md:
- Multiplying two residues below `m` needs `2·log₂ m` bits: with `m ≈ 10^9` use 64-bit products; with `m ≈ 10^18` use 128-bit arithmetic or a multiply-and-reduce routine.
- Start the result at `1 % m`, not `1`: when `m = 1` every power is `0`.
- Negative bases: reduce with `((a % m) + m) % m` first; `%` keeps the sign in C++.

articles.title: Extended Euclidean algorithm
articles.summary: Find gcd(a, b) together with coefficients x, y such that ax + by = gcd(a, b) — and with them, modular inverses.
articles.idea_md:
Euclid's algorithm rests on one fact: a number divides both `a` and `b` exactly when it divides both `b` and `a mod b`. So `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`, and the pair shrinks until the second number is `0`, at which point the first one is the answer.

The extended version also answers *how* the gcd is built from `a` and `b`. Suppose the recursive call already found `x'` and `y'` with

`b·x' + (a mod b)·y' = g`.

Since `a mod b = a − ⌊a / b⌋·b`, substituting and regrouping gives

`a·y' + b·(x' − ⌊a / b⌋·y') = g`,

so `x = y'` and `y = x' − ⌊a / b⌋·y'` work for the original pair. The base case `gcd(a, 0) = a` uses `x = 1, y = 0`.

The payoff is the **modular inverse**. When `gcd(a, m) = 1`, the identity reads `a·x + m·y = 1`, and taking it modulo `m` leaves `a·x ≡ 1`: `x` is the inverse of `a`. The same coefficients solve linear congruences `a·x ≡ c (mod m)` whenever `gcd(a, m)` divides `c`. Both run in `O(log min(a, b))` steps.
articles.formula: a x + b y = \gcd(a, b), \qquad x = y^{\prime}, \quad y = x^{\prime} - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{b} \right\rfloor y^{\prime}
articles.applications_md:
- **Modular inverses** when the modulus is not prime (Fermat's shortcut `a^(m−2)` needs a prime `m`).
- **Linear congruences and Diophantine equations** `a·x + b·y = c`: solvable exactly when `gcd(a, b)` divides `c`.
- **Chinese remainder theorem**: merging `x ≡ r₁ (mod m₁)` and `x ≡ r₂ (mod m₂)` needs an inverse of `m₁` modulo `m₂`.
articles.pitfall_md:
- C++ `%` can be negative for negative operands; normalize with `((a % m) + m) % m` before and after.
- The coefficients can be negative (and large); reduce `x` modulo `m` before using it as an inverse.
- An inverse only exists when `gcd(a, m) = 1` — return a sentinel instead of a wrong number.
- The recursion depth is only `O(log n)`, but an iterative version avoids it entirely if the stack is tight.
